newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Great survivor Haughey ambushed in retirement.
newsitem.headline: Great survivor Haughey ambushed in retirement.

text.p: Charles Haughey, three times prime minister of Ireland, survived scandal and plots to unseat him while in power. He was known as the Great Survivor.
But long after he disappeared from the political pages of the Irish media to be pictured, champagne glass in hand, in the social pages, he was ambushed by a scandal he could not shake.

In November last year, when the Irish Independent newspaper reported that a senior former minister of the Fianna Fail party was the recipient of more than a million pounds from a department store tycoon, the whole nation knew his identity.
It was Haughey, who despite denials first by himself and then through his lawyers, was finally brought before a payments-to-politicians tribunal in Dublin on Tuesday.
Nobody was surprised. His lavish lifestyle, his yacht, private island, stud farm and famed wine cellar had been the talk of Ireland for years.
How, Irish people asked themselves, could a man who began life as an accountant, and earned scarcely more than half a million pounds from his political career, be so wealthy?
It was not a question anyone dared ask Haughey himself. He was ruthless with those who opposed him. Friends and foes were in awe of the man they knew simply as "The Boss".

According to Ben Dunne, the retail store tycoon who donated the mystery 1.3 million pounds ($2 million) between 1989 and 1992, Haughey had financial problems and his aides were trawling for help among a collection of wealthy people who knew him during his time in power.
Dunne told the tribunal that he decided to be the sole benefactor. The reasons were never made clear.
"Here's something for yourself," he recalled telling Haughey when he handed cheques for a quarter of a million to one of the most powerful political figures in the history of modern Ireland.

But Dunne himself was caught up in a family feud over a trust fund set up by the family which owns Dunnes Stores, the green-fronted store prominent in every High Street, and his relatives were querying payments uncovered in an audit.

The family began following the paper trail. It led to payments by Dunne, who was dropped from the family business five years ago after a cocaine and call-girl scandal in Florida, to all major political parties in Ireland.
Michael Lowry, transport minister at the time, resigned in 1996 after admitting that Dunne had paid for the quarter million pound renovation of his private home.
The then prime minister, John Bruton, and leaders of other political parties came forward and acknowledged receiving money from Dunne for campaign funds and election expenses.
But Haughey said nothing.

Apparently believing that silence was security, he continued to say nothing as the tribunal began its work. All the time he was pictured in the Irish media in the landscaped garden of his rural mansion or attending parties for the rich and famous.
But the tribunal began examining mysterious bank accounts in the Cayman Islands tax haven and elsewhere.

Haughey told his lawyers to deny everything. Then he changed his story, telling them he might have received the cash from Dunne. Finally, last week, his lawyers read a statement saying Haughey had misled the tribunal and his legal team. On Tuesday he apologised to the tribunal.
Throughout a 35-year political career, Haughey's skill at escaping from scandal was legendary.
In 1970, he was charged with conspiring to smuggle arms to nationalist guerrillas in Northern Ireland. Though acquitted, he was forced to resign as finance minister.
He clawed his way back to power, taking over as prime minister in 1979. But within 17 months he was out again.
He bounced back in 1982 at the head of a minority government, but mutiny brewed in his Fianna Fail (Soldiers of Destiny) Party and dissidents tried three times to topple him.

Scandals abounded, a man wanted for murder was found in the attorney-general's flat, Haughey's election agent was accused of voting twice and two Dublin journalists had their phones tapped in a 1982 scandal that was to topple him a decade later.

Haughey's last spell in power was from 1987 to 1992. In 1989, with his popularity at an all-time high in opinion polls, he gambled on winning the overall majority that had eluded him. He ended up with four fewer seats than before.
He resigned when former justice minister Sean Doherty said Haughey knew about the wire-tapping of the two journalists, an allegation Haughey forcefully denied until the end.

His retirement appeared to have finally put one of Europe's longest-serving leaders, who dominated Ireland for a decade but was never trusted enough to win an outright majority, out of reach of scandal. Until now.
